utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue, Mr. Knoops, there was a request from the Stanisic Defence that further questions would be put to Dr. Eekhof in relation to the motion for provisional release. Now, the Chamber, having received now the response by -- by the Prosecution, has tried to seek means to have Dr. Eekhof available, but I do understand that he is on leave for quite a while, which means that we can't put any questions. Now, of course we have considered the option of his replacements to be heard, which would be Dr. Rowell, and we have inquired into his availability, and I do understand that he is not unavailable but that he already has reported to -- to the -- how do you say that? -- the director of the detention unit that he will have little to say and that he hardly could comment on the report which was sent in by Dr. Eekhof. Under those circumstances do you still insist on examining a medical doctor on the matter, and would that then be Dr. Rowell?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I deal with the point, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The difficulty we have is that we sought to have Dr. Eekhof give evidence to clear up any residual issues or answers which had not been given by his statement, and so to a certain degree we're in Your Honours' hands as to what Your Honours consider those points might be. So that's the first point I'd make. The second point is this: That it seemed to us that a substantial part of the Prosecution's objections was premised on Mr. Stanisic's personal problems and those that he hopes to sort out and the medical opinion that is premised on that basis. To a certain degree, perhaps, Dr. Rowell could deal with that issue insofar as he could explain how a patient's personal problems, perceived or real, might impact on a psychiatric condition and might, if those personal problems have been resolved, alleviate psychiatric illness and improve the clinical picture. So it's, one, to deal with any points Your Honours might have; and two, to deal with perhaps a generalised issue raised by the Prosecution in their response. So to the extent Your Honours consider that would assist we would seek Dr. Rowell. If Your Honours do not consider that kind of general evidence would assist Your Honours in reaching a decision then obviously we wouldn't want to waste Dr. Rowell's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, and one of the assumption is that the problems would be resolved. That's, of course, rather speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I suppose it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, being close to the ones you have problems with can resolve problems but can make them worse as well. I mean, that's -- I don't know whether this is a medical matter or not, but ... If I do not meet the people with whom have problems they usually do not get any worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My family is the same, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to understand what we can expect and what is medical and what is just common human experience, and that is -- of course, I can imagine that if -- if you resolve all your personal problems, if you have a psychiatric problem, it might be better, I mean, I don't need a doctor for that to tell me that. At the same time, the issue might not be whether good developments in one's personal life may have a beneficial outcome on their psychiatric state that -- but would we then also be again in your own background would that make it worse? I mean, there's a lot of speculation. There's a lot of assumptions to which I'm not yet confident that the medical profession could give -- could give answers unless the answers would go in all directions. I can expect you to would say, if this is the case then it would be better. If that's the case, it might be worse and whether we are talking about this or that. We just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There is -- I understand what Your Honour's saying and I'm not going to pursue the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether the Stanisic Defence insists on -- insists on examining Dr. Rowell, and we were informed that he'll -- if at all, he can comment on the report of his colleague that it would be very little. The Chamber's not very much inclined with this report to seek to further examine Dr. Rowell, but if the Stanisic Defence thinks that's the appropriate way to proceed, then the Chamber will consider up to a certain moment whether it's -- it provides any answers which would assist us, and if it would not provide us with such answers in the first five minutes, then it would not be provide us with such answers in the minutes to follow either. So we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I just consult with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just raise one more possible question and if I may then leave it with Your Honours to decide whether that's a pivotal issue for you, and it's the issue of how, given what Dr. Rowell has read in relation to Mr. Stanisic's condition, how likely is it that within a two-week period or two- to three-week period that there would be any real deterioration in the accused's medical condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Jordash, we are not going to say what are the pivotal issues for us. You bring your case as you wish. As I said before, if you do not insist, the Chamber, certainly in view of the report it has received, doesn't expect that much. If you take a different position, if you think that it's nevertheless worthwhile to take the time with Dr. Rowell, and if you think that you really can produce any further statements which would bring us any further, you have the first five minutes to -- to prove that such a thing can come out, and if not then the Chamber considers that the answer that he would not really be in a position to comment on what his colleagues reported, and -- his colleague reported and that most likely he has little to say about it would be the final statement on the matter. I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have to, from the Defence perspective, be super cautious then and call doctor -- the doctor to be questioned on that issue since we see it as the pivotal issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And let's just check whether at this moment Dr. Rowell is available or not or would it be only later. And as again I said, if the first five minutes result in, I can't say that or I wouldn't comment on that or I have insufficient information, then it's really done. Dr. Rowell will be available later today and most likely here in the courtroom. So then I move on to the next matter which is the practicalities of the examination of the next witness. The next witness enjoys protective measures, being face distortion and voice distortion and pseudonym. Now, we already experienced last time that there are problems in having the audio available for Mr. Stanisic. That problem has not been resolved. That problem will be resolved, but the technicians need the winter recess to put in to place all the technical facilities which allow Mr. Stanisic to receive audio, whether distorted or original, in a language he understands. We have several options at this moment. The first option is that we decide that the testimony will not be given in public. We would then make it closed session and then we do not need the voice distortion any further, which would also mean that at a later stage only the transcript could be made public, not the audio, not the video, because it would be undistorted. It would be the real voice of the witness. That is quite a price to be paid. The second option is that Mr. Stanisic, of which we do understand that he understands some English, either listens to the English booth, which of course is not distorted, or that he reads from the screen the transcript which gives the English text of the testimony. I must say that I have and the Chamber has not yet been fully informed about the level of mastering the English language by Mr. Stanisic. I'm not aware of it. If we would proceed in this way, the full audio and video also in his own language would be available to Mr. Stanisic soon after the hearing. The third option, of course, would be that Mr. Stanisic decides to attend the proceedings in this courtroom. I would say the last weeks the medical reports always have been that Mr. Stanisic is able to be transported to the courtroom and to attend court here. He has chosen not to do so. Well, we are here facing some consequences of that decision. I'd like to hear from the parties how they wish to proceed, and since the public character of the trial is involved as well, it's not only that Mr. Stanisic but Mr. Simatovic bears the consequences of our decision and so does the Prosecution, but as the most interested party and perhaps the party who could give the key to the solution, I invite you, Mr. Knoops and Mr. Jordash, to give your views on the several options we have, briefly, which would be the best to pursue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we first have a small break to confer with Mr. Stanisic before we make a decision on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, we could hear from the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution can think of no other alternatives other than those set out by the Chamber and would submit that the reverse order, namely the last one is obviously the most ideal, followed by the second one where Mr. Stanisic would hear the testimony in English, and as a final solution the possibility of having the session in private session with only the transcript being made public at a later date. I'm not sure if the Chamber has explored with the technical people whether they would be able to, after the fact, put on voice distortion, but I myself do not know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have thought about it, and I have not discussed it with our technical people. Unless we get a quick and a clear yes, it's no -- it's of no -- it doesn't make sense to further explore it, because the next witness to appear will testify in closed session anyhow, and after the recess the matter will be resolved. So unless we get a clear and immediate yes, we should not further investigate the possibility because it would take us the whole afternoon and it's not what we could afford at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. While the Stanisic Defence is consulting with Mr. Stanisic, a very much related problem -- a very much related problem and one I would ask the Chamber to address with the technical people, is that we have been informed earlier that it is impossible to do a videolink witness white the videolink is being used with Mr. Stanisic. I would ask the Chamber to perhaps explore with the technical people whether changes to the system can be made over the winter break. The Prosecution will be applying for the taking of some evidence via videolink for a couple of elderly and infirm witnesses that we don't believe are able to travel to The Hague, and that application should be submitted next week before the winter break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's videolink with the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- I take it that you -- you know that we need usually a little bit over a week to prepare for that. An application should be made, reasons to be given. We'll then hear from the other parties whether there's any -- that goes the usual way of motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I intend to do that next week for the witnesses that we intend to call at the end of February. So hopefully there is enough time for that. But just to see what the Chamber is talking about the technical limitations of the videolink, one of the limitations we've been told about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that we have then the practical problems of two videolinks at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's perhaps also something for the Stanisic Defence to think about, but -- yes, two videolinks. We need more screens at our desks. Yes. Mr. Knoops -- Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, having spoken to Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Stanisic makes two points which is, one, that notwithstanding the medical evidence, he's choosing to stay in the video room because he perceives that the logistics of bringing him to court would tire him out more and the trial sessions may have to then be shorter, and so he's doing what in his mind he sees as something which will assist in keeping the trial moving. And the second point is relating to the first, that he would be content for this witness to be heard -- for him to hear this witness in English and listen to the audiotapes at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And not to give up the public character of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Indeed. That was his concern too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the suggested solution, Mr. Petrovic, any further comments, because that's of course where the Simatovic Defence would lose the public character of the trial, but that seems now to be -- at least Mr. Stanisic does not oppose against --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the option that the Stanisic Defence team has proposed, I believe, is the most useful and technically doable, and I think that we should proceed in that manner today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber decides that we'll proceed with the next witness with face and voice distortion and a pseudonym. This follows from the earlier decision on protective measures by another Trial Chamber, which actually means that Mr. Stanisic can follow the proceedings in English audio. He has a screen on which he can read the English text, and in view of the fact that he has expressed his preference to proceed in this way, the Chamber will follow that suggestion. And again, full video and audio in his own language will be available very soon to Mr. Stanisic. Then in view of any other procedural matter -- if not, then, Madam Usher, you're invited to escort the witness into the courtroom. Could I remind all parties that they should switch off their microphones when the witness answers a question. Whenever any portion of the evidence or even in the beginning pseudonym sheets, et cetera, would create any risk of revealing the identity of the witness to the public, then the parties should ask for private session. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And if I may introduce to the Chamber Mr. Amir Zec, who will be taking the evidence of the next witness on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have to move in private session right away or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Before we start, today we're going to talk about Zvornik, and we have in our binder of maps, map 27 we would like to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour if we could go into private session, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- get my current thinking on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Don't repeat those words, please, because it reveals already an aspect which we -- which we kept confidential. If you want to -- could you produce or strike out just the irrelevant part. And if you add to that your initials, then it is clear that it was you who did it and not someone else at a later stage. Yes. Madam Usher, could you assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it please the Court, I will conduct my examination in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam. Madam, can you see the piece of paper in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you see -- can you see your name on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Is this your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you also see the date of birth on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after this sheet is shown to the parties, we would then admit it into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has already been shown to the parties. Mr. Registrar, this would be what number --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: For that I would like to ask the witness to sign the paper if it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Practice is different in different courtrooms, but at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam -- Madam JF-007, could you please sign the piece of paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P110 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P110 is admitted under seal. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, whenever I put a question to you, could you please wait for a few moments and give me time to finish my question and then you start answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because I'm going to deal with prior evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I suggest that -- you said you would want to go into private session since that's not on the transcript, and it is because you started putting your question before the answer had been translated. So the instructions for the witness, take them seriously yourself as well, Mr. Zec. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam, do you remember that you already testified --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, did you provide a statement to the investigators of this Tribunal on the 29th September 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I provided a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Before your evidence in the Milosevic case was the 1996 statement read out to you, and did you explain some of the parts of the statement in the addendum to that statement provided on the 23rd September 2003?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything was clear to me. I provided accurate answers, and I speak the truth to this very day and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would like ask that 65 ter 5194 with ERN number 2 -- 02299395 to 02299400 be called up on the screen, please. And of course no broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, did you have an occasion to review your 1996 statement and the addendum to that statement provided in 2003 before you came to give evidence today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I looked at everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if you can scroll down on this English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam JF-007, do you see before you on the screen something? Can you recognise your signature on what you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we please go now to last page of this document. If you can scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam JF-007, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Could now the Prosecution call 65 ter 5195 with ERN number 03365020 to 03365021, and if we can go to the second page, to the bottom. And of course no broadcast for this document as well. If we can go to second page. Can we blow up little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Please scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the screen once again. Do you recognise the signature on this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders the statement of this witness dated 27, 28, and 27, 29 September 1996 [sic] as the 65 ter 5194 and the addendum statement dated 3rd September 2003, 65 ter 5195 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 5194 will be Exhibit Number P113 under seal, and 65 ter 5195 will be Exhibit Number P114 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Both are admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point the Prosecution tenders also three associate exhibits to this 92 filing. They are 65 ter 2 -- 2827 and 2828 under seal, and Exhibit 65 ter 5196. And also, I would like to inform the Chamber that Stanisic Defence did not have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the -- I do not hear of any objections from the Simatovic Defence, so therefore these two documents can be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, exhibit number -- 65 ter 2527 will be Exhibit Number P115 MFI, and 65 ter 2828 will be Exhibit Number P116 MFI, and 65 ter 5196 will be Exhibit Number P117 MFI, all under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could I just have on the screen not to be shown to the public for one second the redacted version of the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there's any confusion these are exhibits associated to 92 ter filing, so they're not statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that. Is this the -- this is not the redacted version, is it? I'd like to check the redactions, or is this the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: There is not -- Your Honour, there are no redactions on the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, they're all admitted under seal. And you have no public versions? The MFI'd ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just a bit confused about the numbering and what the documents were because they were not all shown on the screen, but I do understand that there's no redacted version, or you do not intend to tender a redacted version of the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will provide -- we will provide redacted versions to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But I was a bit mistaken when I said they to be MFI'd, because these were exhibits that should be admitted into evidence. We'll deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I made a mistake. P115, P116, and P117 are admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, you were right. I didn't ask that statement and addendum to be admitted, redacted version and public version, so we will do -- we will provide the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll deal with that later then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just clarification on page 20 in today's transcript. Exhibit P number 115 is make -- made -- there was a reference to a 65 ter 2527. It should be 2827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And also the last exhibit which was admitted, P117 is a public version. It's not under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a look at it and then we'll most likely change the status.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam JF-007, in your statement of 1996, you talk about an incident that took place on the 9th of April, 1992, at around 10.00 when a group of soldiers stormed your shelter and took the men out. On page 3, you say, and I quote: "Some ten soldiers stormed the premises wearing camouflage uniforms, woolen hats on their heads, and threatening us with long-barrelled rifles. They had masks with slits for the eyes and mouth, and some of them wore black gloves with the fingers cut off. By their dialect, I concluded that they were from Serbia." When you gave that statement in 1996 to the investigators, you showed them some photographs -- or, rather, the investigators showed you some photographs, and I would like to show you one of those photographs now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could have 65 -- I'm sorry, it's now P117 up on the screen. It should be page 11. Can we go to previous page? It should be with ERN 00400125. I'm sorry, 00400152.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam JF-007, when you saw this photograph in 1996, you said, and I quote: "The masks that these soldiers are wearing are identical to the soldiers that came to our basement." And that is on page 5 of that statement. My question to you today is this: When you look at this photograph now, do you have any doubt at all that these are the identical masks, just like the soldiers wore who took your menfolk out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are. And also those --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the photograph, can you tell us what building this is that they're in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: How do you -- are you able to recognise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the -- looking at the carpets and the stairs going up to the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to show you a video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 4529 -- I'm sorry, the Prosecution will play a clip from 65 ter 4592. This is a video-clip from video-tape with ERN V000-0534, and the clip starts at the time code 00:29:55 and goes up to 00:31:30, and I would like to stop this clip at 00:31:11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before it will be played, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Simatovic Defence objects to the use of this video with this witness. The video contains elements which have nothing to do with the testimony of this witness, and we'll be able to see that if you look at the video. First of all, there's something from an unknown location, then there's a location in Brsadin which is Eastern Slavonia October 1991, then some footage from November 1991, the Serbian guards staff, some training centre, et cetera. So I object to the use of this video if it has any other purpose except to ask the witness whether she can recognise an individual on the footage, and she'll find it easier to do that looking at the photographs being shown, the photographs attached to her statement. Now, if the Prosecutor wants to use this video for any other purpose and in any other way, then I consider that there is no link between that video and this witness and nothing that this witness can tell us will relate to that link so I'm -- I am objecting to the video being shown. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's a conditional objection. I do understand, because not under all circumstances you object. It depends on what questions will be put in relation to ... Mr. Zec, could you respond to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the video will be played for the witness to -- for identification. She will say what she can recognise, and I'll -- I -- it seems to me it will be helpful for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is about persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Including persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the objection does not stand, I take it, Mr. Zec, because it's not about where it is, when it is, but about persons. Therefore, the video may be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very brief description. This is a clip containing a footage from Eastern Slavonia in August 1991. And for the benefit of the booth, this is the transcript of clip one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "MB: In an area close to the Osijek front line, these irregulars who call themselves the Serbian Tigers are practising what a short time ago they were actually doing - the capture of Croatian-held villages. They are separate from the army, but usually take its orders. No peace plan can work unless it has their approval and, at the moment, their commander is talking peace. This force is the likely foundation of a Serbian Army: It is better trained, better motivated, better turned out than the regular troops with whom it has a rather tense relationship. Yet under the peace plan, the irregulars would either be disbanded or asked to serve as policemen alongside the Croats they are now fighting against. To them, that's on the edge of the unbelievable. "ZRA: Big problem is, and the only problem - we don't trust each other. That's true. We can't trust them and they can't trust us any more. We are going to prepare ourselves because we do know that they are going to attack us. So we are going to defend these people here again. That's what I think personally. I don't believe much in this peace. I would like to believe 100 per cent, but as I told you, we are going to do our best to keep this peace and keep Mr. Cyrus Vance satisfied."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, can you tell us what this footage shows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It shows that Arkan tried allegedly to make the peace, but that was just a trick, because on the 8th of April, he was in Mali Zvornik, in the hotel there, and that's (redacted). You can see that hotel across the Drina River, and allegedly he wanted to contribute to peace, that they should hand over their weapons, that there should be calm, but all that was just a trick.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned one particular person. That means that you recognised him on the video, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what those soldiers were doing there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Can the question be more specified, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean what the soldiers were doing on the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Whereas the Defence objected against the line of questioning, the Prosecution clearly announced that it would use the clip only for identification. The events on the clip go back to 1991. The witness has not knowledge on the events in 1991. At the least there is no foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last question was withdrawn, Mr. Knoops. Let's see what other questions there are, because I could imagine that if the -- if -- I'll refrain from commenting at this moment since we're in open session. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, could you see this footage on television?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I was asking you, this footage that we saw earlier on, could you see that kind of footage on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992. It was at the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you know which television channel or station that was on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, we saw these soldiers wearing masks over their heads. To the best of your recollections, the soldiers that stormed your basement, were they wearing masks like that or similar masks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one -- masks like that. You could just see the slits for their eyes and mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting my learned friend, Your Honour, but this is leading the witness as far as I can see the way that question was formulated. It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we all saw these mask on the clip, so I can go step-by-step. That is no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, by showing it on the clip and then to say, "Is this what it was," is, of course, leading, but at the same time, Mr. Petrovic, have you ever seen some woolen thing on someone's head with where -- well, it's with the eyes, which looked any different from what we see here? I would say it's rather a superfluous question, because if the question would not have been put to the witness, that's what would have been on my mind as what the witness has described. So let's -- or have you ever seen any other -- they call them balaclavas, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there we are. Useless question, useless intervention. Perhaps useless decision as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, on this footage we saw soldiers wearing masks over their heads. To the best of your recollections, did the soldiers who stormed your basement have masks like that or similar ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly the same ones like this. Black with slits for the eyes and mouth. Exactly the same ones. And if you were to ask a child, a child could tell you that and explain what they were wearing, that that was the case. Any child you happened to ask would say the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders into evidence 65 ter -- Exhibit 54929 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's the video, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And on the transcript it should be 4529.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. President, no objection except for the text of the British reporter because that relates to opinion evidence. So that, in our opinion, should be redacted. Otherwise, no objection to the tendering of the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, apparently the objection is based on the thought that what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It's not about an objection. It's just to alert the Court that Mr. Stanisic requests to go to the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it's -- anyway, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He's content for the proceedings to continue if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then we'll continue, although wouldn't it be wise -- we said three times five quarters of an hour, half an hour break. That would be approximately this moment. But let's perhaps first deal with the -- deal with the objection, although ... Mr. Knoops, apparently the objection is based on the comments to be taken for the truth of the content of that opinion of the journalist, and the redaction to be made both on the video material, and what exactly are the words you're so concerned about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's just a small text spoken by the British journalist when he explains about the strength of the army, et cetera. I believe now the Prosecution intends to tender the document just for identification purposes. That it should not be proper that such a comment which relates to opinion evidence should be included in the document. So the Defence suggests that Prosecution is allowed to tender the video-clip in it's entirety except for those two or three lines which relate to this opinion evidence given by this British reporter on military equipment, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've been listening to the English. Has the text you referred for the booth to -- to portions of the transcript? I didn't follow whether it has been translated and whether it appears -- whether the English text appears on the transcript at this moment. I'm just trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the clip itself is in English, so the reporter is speaking English, and I think it was captured on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it. I see it. Video-clip played.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your mike again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your objection is denied, Mr. Knoops, primarily for the following reason: If the witness says that this is what she watched on television, then at least we should know what she watched on television. It would even be beneficial to know to what extent her opinion or whatever she thought may have been influenced by what she saw on television. Now, if there's any concern that on the basis of what this reporter says that the Chamber would take it for that reason for the truth of its content, the Chamber is not -- not to say that under all circumstances we cannot exclude from the possibility that if it was perceived at that moment by a journalist, that if that fits in well to other matters we might not ignore it, but certainly not to accept matters on the basis of what apparently is the opinion of one single journalist. Therefore, the objection is denied. Mr. Registrar, the video-clip would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be exhibit number P118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just check because -- and verify that the French booth has translated all the words spoken. I would have to switch to the French channel in order to find the answer. Because I think we -- we practiced this earlier, the procedure for any video played, any video with text, is the following: The booth should be provided with a transcript of the words spoken. Since the spoken language is often very quick, translation will be done exceptionally on the basis of the written transcript if it goes too quick, and then one of our translators, one of the interpreters, follows whether what is transcribed reflects what is said, whereas the other interpreter translates the words at that time then read by him or her. There is a risk that we have an incomplete French transcript in this respect. We'll verify that during the break. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, please proceed. And I think -- I still have to give a decision on admission of the video. I explained why the objection was denied, but I don't think we had admitted the video already in evidence. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The video will be Exhibit P118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In your evidence you said that you found shelter in your cellar a few days before the 9th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, if I may just -- we took a break, Mr. Knoops, at the time when Mr. Stanisic needed to be absent. I don't see him being -- having returned. I do not know whether that's -- whether there's any -- there we are. Mr. Stanisic, I just noticed that you had not yet returned, so we took a minute to wait until you were present again. Mr. Zec, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, during that period could you hear rifle shots across the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: During the same period before you found shelter and after that, did you have an occasion to see troops, tanks, and other such things moving around the town of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would like to show you another video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the Prosecution calls video-clip 65 ter 4508, starting at the time code 00:02:33. It goes to up 00:30:00, and this is a BBC report from 1992. For the benefit of the booth, this is transcript clip number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam JF-007, can you see the beginning of the clip on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: What do you see on the screen then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you see a river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see a river in front of the houses. Several houses and above them a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the town in the photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you tell us from which perspective are we seeing Zvornik in this photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Serbia. The photo was taken from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would like to play the clip now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And channel 5 I usually receive French translation, but for the last ten lines I haven't heard anything, so I would like to verify whether there's any technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you play the clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still -- on channel 5 I do not receive any -- apparently there has been a problem over the last 15 lines. I think that Mr. Zec just verified with the witness whether she could -- whether she could see on the screen what seems to be the opening scene of the video footage. That is a river as the witness said taken from the Serbian side before the houses. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay. Can we play the video now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "Reporter: Tanks crossed the river into the town and although the situation there is confused, it seems that the newly independent Bosnians have lost control of another part of their country. Their president complained of aggression by the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we restart. I do not hear any French translation on channel 5. I don't know what is happening, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we verify whether now the French translation is -- yes, I do hear you now. [French spoken] Which creates a bit of a problem. Could I have a look at what you distributed for the -- for the booth as video-clip 2. I do understand that it's all right now. Then could the video-clip be played on -- from the beginning again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Reporter: The civil war spread this morning to Zvornik on the banks of the River Drina. Serbian irregulars have threatened to capture the town unless the Muslims gave up their arms. Eventually, it was the federal army which moved in. ... although the situation there is confused, it seems that the newly independent Bosnians have lost control of another part of their country. Their president complained of aggression by the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the sequence of the portions of the video are mixed up in what has been provided to the booth. I heard translation at least now of page 34, line 25, up to and including page 35, line 3, and then it continues: "Although the situation there is confused, it seems that the newly independent Bosnians have lost control over another part of their country. Their president complained of aggression by the Serbs." Although I think I heard portions of this already earlier, but we now at least have a more or less complete transcript. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will repeat. I would like to ask witness some specific questions about some specific portions of this video. The first portion is at 00:13 of this particular clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam JF-007, do you see a photo or an image on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you see the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what river it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the Drina River, and you can also see Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: According to what you remember, the two soldiers, what side of the Drina are they on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And Zvornik -- and Bosnia-Herzegovina should be on the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The second portion I would like to show to the witness is on 00:27 -- 24 seconds of this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam JF-007, do you see a bridge on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Karakaj bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Is it true that this bridge connects Mali Zvornik and Zvornik, meaning Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders into evidence 65 ter Exhibit 4508.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any objections? And that is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit Number P119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 65 ter -- is that the video? That's the second clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will tender the clip, video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And since there are no objections, apparently, Mr. Registrar, P119 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Zec, I'm still asking myself is there any dispute about this bridge being the Karakaj bridge? Is there any dispute about -- would the case have been any different if these two soldiers would have been on the other side of the river? I'm trying to understand what I'm listening to and what is in dispute and what is not in dispute, and I take it that at the time the war was reported on television, but I mean, if it had been on the other side of the bridge would it have changed anything in the case in the other side of the river?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the trial it will be more clear the reason why we're showing this particular clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll see. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I would like now to play another clip which is 65 ter 4508, and this one is starting at time code 00:05:03 and goes up to 00:08:08. I will stop at time code 00:07:20. And for the benefit of the booth, it is transcript with clip number -- number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: Serbian irregulars in action in Zvornik, a town that used to be mixed, and used to be peaceful. Today, it wasn't either. These were not men of the Yugoslav army, but of the most disciplined of the Serbian militias under commander Arkan. They were mopping up the last of Muslim resistance. The Bosnian authorities, mainly Muslim, were driven out of the town. They put their total dead at at least 300. That may be an exaggeration, but casualties were certainly heavy. The Serbs are now doing in Bosnian what they did last year in Croatia which is on an argument of self-defence to extend their control into formally mixed areas. In fact, they're making Greater Serbia happen. In a village 2 miles south of Zvornik, we came upon the human calamity which is the practical result of all this. Two thousand Muslims are stranded and struggling to get out. They spoke of the fighting they'd left behind them, the murder and hostage taking which went with it. "Unknown Man: Terrible things are happening now. They have been happening since two, three days. It's a terrible terrible terror which has been made, and which is being made right now. You can hear even now some shells. "Reporter: ... refugees waiting for rescue. The artillery barrage was creeping towards us in the villages on the Muslim side of Zvornik. "Interpreter: [Voiceover] We don't have any arms ... "Unknown Man: ... they are firing at us. "Reporter: He begged [indiscernible] to help them against the aggression of the Serbs and the Federal Army. The cry as we leave is again for help as quickly as possible, and the applause is only because we are the first sign they've had in days that anyone out there cares about their plight. Numbers are difficult to estimate, but in single file, on mountain parts, and great columns on the wider tracks, it's possible that as many as 20.000 people are on the move, most of them by foot. These have been walking for two days. They had gone 18 miles, had at least another 20 to go along this trail of tears. They were heading for the safety of a Muslim area ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's now that the French translation has completed, Mr. Zec, and even parts that could not -- apparently not be transcribed are now translated and on the French channel. I couldn't repeat the words, but apparently there's more on the transcript you provided than what was transcribed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will later be completed. That's always the problem with spoken text and video. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My understanding was that we provided to the booths exactly portions we want to play and exactly that parts but transcripts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be that it goes so quick that transcribing it here in court is almost impossible. Have you provided the transcript also to our transcriber in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes from the English booth that the tape stopped before the end of the paragraph that was transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, apparently more text has been given to the booth than that was played. We're not going to resolve this right away, but I insist on great accuracy in this respect. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, did you recognise the area or the place where the refugees had gathered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could only be Snagovo or the area leading towards Josanica. I personally wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: How far is Snagovo from Zvornik approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 7 to 9 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Again, I would like now to show to -- to witness some specific portions of this video, and I will ask specific questions. So the first portion I'd like to show is on -- in this clip at 00:27.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam JF-007, do you recognise the place where this shot was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the department store in the direction Bire [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, microphone, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of the street was Bire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So next portion I would like to show to the witness is -- portion is on 00:24.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam JF-007, do you recognise the place where this shot was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The centre of Zvornik? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise the mosque, the buildings there. I recognise all. This is in the direction of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this 65 ter 4508, which is a video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: With the exception that we object to the introduction of the place called Snagovo, because it wasn't in the evidence previously released by the Prosecution, and the witness was not able to establish a link between that video-clip and her direct knowledge. She literally testified that she wasn't there and she assumed it was Snagovo. Above that, it's -- it was not early in the evidence. There was no foundation for the introduction of that city and the alleged crimes there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, I leave it to you whether you want to further find out about it or I don't know how important it is for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Madam JF-007, when you mentioned the village where refugees had gathered and when you said that it was Snagovo, how did you recognise the village? If you want me so, I can bring the photo back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could recognise the village because I had gone through Snagovo that way before the new motorway to Tuzla was built, and most of the people fled through that area. They took that road, went up to the forest, and then proceeded from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the objection stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In so far that's -- the objection also relates to the fact that this is new evidence. It was never introduced by the Prosecution that Snagovo would be part of the witness evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this goes to the deportation, and it's showing people moving out. I just asked the witness if she recognised the village where the people are and she provided her answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Mr. Registrar, the video would receive.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video would be Exhibit Number P120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Witness, you were seeking -- is there anything you'd like to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we lived in Zvornik, then the place was called Snagovo. Later on they renamed it, and the clip did depict what was known as Snagovo. I could recognise it. I know it well. There were a lot of things in the photo that I recognised as being in Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this concludes my examination. Thank you very much for listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zec. What will be the sequence of cross-examination? Stanisic Defence first?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, also in your own interest, Dr. Rowell will be available on from approximately 5.30, and he'll be available for a relatively short period of time. I do not know -- I made a mistake. He'll be available after 6.00, approximately 6.30. He might be a bit earlier and he is limited in his time. May I take it that cross-examination will be concluded by then, also looking at the Simatovic Defence? Let's get started and see how far we come. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness JF-007, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Knoops, and Mr. Knoops is counsel for Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much for joining us today despite the circumstances. First of all, could we call up P119, please, the video-clip, again. I believe it's not P119. It's P120. Yes. Could -- if it could be stopped, please, there. Can it be stopped there, please. Witness, the video-clip mentions here: "Eventually it was the federal army which moved in." Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness could not read that. I can imagine that she may have heard it. The commentator said, "... it was the federal army which moved in," for your information. Now, your question Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that the federal army moved in to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav, you mean. The Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Do you agree that the -- the tank which is still on the video screen was a tank from the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm certain. One hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did you see more tanks of the Yugoslav Army on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could you give us a rough estimation as to how many tanks of the Yugoslav Army you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that those tanks were accompanied by soldiers of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that the Yugoslav Army was part of the attack on Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that Mr. Dragan Nikolic was a JNA commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was. And I was -- I personally went to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: How did you know that he was -- belonged to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he and his soldiers were put up in a company in Karakaj, on the premises of company in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could you indicate to us where Karakaj is -- is -- exactly where it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karakaj is when you go from Tuzla, Bijeljina, towards Zvornik. Karakaj comes first, and then 3 kilometres later you reach Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's where there's a Serbian cemetery. That's where Karakaj is. There's a Serbian cemetery there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that the soldiers from this company in Karakaj were involved in the attack on Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. One was going to kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise uniforms of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Green camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You just testified that you spoke to Mr. Dragan Nikolai [sic]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: During this conversation did he indicate to you that he was in fact involved in the attack on Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that your late husband worked for a company in Zvornik? Sorry. Maybe we could go into closed session at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Private session and closed session is more or less the same here. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Witness, upon your return to Zvornik, whom did you see in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned on the eighth day. I just went to search for some trace of my -- but I didn't go back to live there nor could you go back to live there. We reached Karakaj first, and then we went to see Dragan Nikolic and he sent us off to Zvornik. He told us to go to Zvornik. First of all he said -- well, (redacted) was her name, and he said to us, "If they didn't have any weapons, then they probably were in battle somewhere. If they had weapons," we said "they wouldn't have been in the shelter, they would have been in the woods like you." And he said, "Well, we'll look at the list. We have a list, and we'll look to see who was alive, who was captured, and who was killed," and he ordered a soldier to go and bring those papers. He looked at them and then he said, "He's not on the list, not among the captured or the killed." And he said, "They must have escaped somewhere and taken to the woods." Now, how could they have taken to the woods when they surrounded them and put them up against a wall? But anyway he said, "Go and talk to the president." And we went to talk to Grujic, and Grujic said that we could go to the flat --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise. I think that goes beyond the question. Sorry to interrupt you. My question is: Is it correct that upon your return to Zvornik, you saw JNA soldiers killing people in Zvornik? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were dead people all over the place, our people, women, children. They were all over. Yes, they did kill them, yes. They tried to kill us, too, when we went to look for our -- our folk. That same man, Dragan, sent a truck, and there were four of them, and they got to the building before we arrived on foot. So we came across one of these four at the entrance to the house by the staircase, and the other three were taking things out of the car, out of the truck, various material and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Madam, would -- I don't want to be impolite, but my question is simply: Do you recall that after your return to Zvornik you saw JNA soldiers still around in Zvornik killing civilians? If you could please answer the question with yes or no, that might be helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops. Mr. Petrovic, will it be you? Witness JF-007, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic, and you'll see him to your left, standing. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness JF-007, I would, first of all, like on behalf of Mr. Simatovic and this Defence team to express our condolences for the great loss that you had suffered in the situation that you were in and that you testified about here today, and I'm just going to ask you a few questions that are just directed at elucidating some of the important circumstances, circumstances important to these proceedings and not anything else, not to question anything else in any way, not to question and challenge the tragedy that happened to you that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Witness, if you'd like to say something about the -- about the matter we just discussed before we went into private session, then I think it would be good to return into private session. Is it about this or is it about anything else that you'd like to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something about the government and authorities with regard to the claim that I provided a statement to the authorities. Why don't you invite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. We return into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Witness JF-007, you've answered all the questions that were put to you, that were questions put to you by the parties and questions, although only a few, by the Bench. The Chamber fully understands how difficult it must be to come and tell about events you have described, and of course which must have a huge impact on your life. The Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for giving this testimony, and we wish that you have a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I'd like to add something if I may. May I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Say a word, if it is an appropriate word in a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear enough from what you said that you do not recognise that. If there are any further questions in relation to that, the Chamber will carefully look at it. We have -- until this moment we have not finally decided on any such matter. Anything else? If not, I wish you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They can ask my government, my government, not the Serbian government, whether I gave a statement or not. Just that, because it's painful for me that question, just as the fact that my children were killed is painful to me. I don't like people saying that I gave a statement to some government or some authority. So that is what I have said and will say again and again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for adding this. You're invited to follow Madam Usher, and again, a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Knoops would like to put a few questions to the doctor who is replacing Dr. Eekhof. The doctor would arrive at approximately 6.00, and he has to leave rather quickly. Would a break of 20 minutes do as far as you're concerned? And I take it that once we have heard the doctor, that the session would be relatively short, that is, depending on what answers we get, anything between five and 12 or 13 minutes. Would a short break do so as in order to have the doctor not to wait too long? THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to ask you to give me a 15-minute break so that I could rest a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 25 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Rowell. First of all, thank you for coming so quickly to the courtroom. May I again inquire with the parties whether there's any need to take a solemn declaration from the doctor? We haven't done until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not believe there is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I see that Defence agrees with that. Dr. Rowell, Dr. Eekhof has made a -- two reports, the first one dated 20th of November, the other one dated the 2nd of December, 2009, which were attached to a motion for provisional release filed by the Stanisic Defence. The Stanisic Defence, although being aware that you were not the doctor who made these statements, nevertheless today said that it would insist on putting further questions to you. The Chamber had inquired whether you would be available or not. The response we got is that it might be very difficult for you to comment on reports written by one of your colleagues and that you might have very little to say, but the Chamber, where the Stanisic Defence insisted on putting further questions to you, the Chamber did not want to deny such a request. Therefore, Mr. Jordash, I take it will have some questions for you. Whether there will be any follow-up questions by the others is still to be seen, but I see Mr. Jordash on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for coming, and we do appreciate your attendance here. Could I just ask a few questions, and I won't be long, and I do, of course, appreciate that you're coming into this late. Firstly, could I just try to understand how familiar you are with Mr. Stanisic's medical file. DR. ROWELL: I have read his file today and a few months ago when I previously acted as reporting medical officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you on that first occasion or this occasion have the opportunity to speak to any of the treating doctors or to Dr. Eekhof? DR. ROWELL: I briefly spoke with Dr. Eekhof today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you able to speak to Dr. Eekhof about the basis for his opinion? DR. ROWELL: No. I've only read the records in the medical file.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But you weren't able to speak to him -- what did you speak to him about? You didn't speak to him about the -- DR. ROWELL: I spoke to him about his frozen motorbike, which was stuck at the gaol, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I saw him as well, actually, had the same conversation. You will have observed in the medical file, I take it, Mr. Stanisic's steady improvement since returning to UNDU on the 4th of May, 2009. DR. ROWELL: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And steady -- is it right that that steady movement has been both in relation to his physical illness and his psychological illness? DR. ROWELL: He's had improvement in both from the personal aspect since I saw him the first time and more recently. The most significant improvement is psychological. It appears that his physical illness is relatively stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And have you read the two reports filed by Dr. Eekhof, one dated the 20th of November and one the 2nd of December? DR. ROWELL: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm just going to refer to the one on the 20th of November, 2009, and Dr. Eekhof's view -- or I should say Dr. Petrovic's and Dr. Eekhof's view that solving some of these important problems that Mr. Stanisic has reported to the doctors will lead to diminishing stress and consequently lead to improvement of Mr. -- I've just been reminded that if we're going to veer into the issue of Mr. Stanisic's personal issues, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Personal circumstances are not for public.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Finally, Doctor, this: Having observed his -- Mr. Stanisic's medical records and the improvements which have taken place over the last seven months, are you able to give the Court any indication as to the solidity of those improvements? What I mean is this: We've asked for provisional release for four weeks. What are the risks given this medical progression of a deterioration, significant or otherwise, in the space of four weeks? DR. ROWELL: Unfortunately, I don't think I would be able to speculate with any degree of certainty. He is definitely better psychologically since a change in his medication, and perhaps a slight change in approach at the detention unit, and he certainly has a greater capability to deal with stressors and his day-to-day life in a way. So I think that he is more capable than what he has been in the past. Whether that overwhelms him or not, the only way to tell would be to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
