utterances.text: Would your answer be the same if I put to you a period of two weeks? DR. ROWELL: I don't think it would make any difference. I don't think I could really comment knowing him and his capacity to -- to deal with those issues. If things went well, then the time could be longer. If things went poorly right from the start, then the time would be shorter. So even the time is -- you'd have to wait and see. You'd have to try it and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the last -- the last question, I think -- perhaps it hypothetical, but I'll try. Would any deterioration be observable, and could that be reported immediately to the Trial Chamber? DR. ROWELL: Well, I think it would be observable, yes. He would regress from his current state. The person who was making the assessment would have to assess him beforehand to have some sort of reference value against which to judge whether he's coping well or not coping well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to offer any sensible or safe -- no. Let me start that again. Would reporting several times a week deal with that eventuality, picking up observable signs of deterioration so that action could be taken at the Trial Chamber level? DR. ROWELL: I'm not sure what you mean, but if he was regularly assessed, you could tell whether this activity was causing him to deteriorate and could be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thankfully your answer was clear than my question. Thank you very much, Doctor. I've got nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we try to keep it short because we know the doctor has an appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm do my best, doctor. Doctor without going into the nature of the personal problems the record records you as saying "He, meaning Mr. Stanisic, claims that they are a significant component and it's very difficult to say otherwise." Can I take from that that a large part of the assessment of the role that the personal problems play in Mr. Stanisic's overall health is Mr. Stanisic's own opinion that they do? DR. ROWELL: Yes, and no. When -- as a clinician, the first time I see a patient and I have relatively little knowledge of their background, I have to go on what they tell me. That is the primary indication. The more you get to know somebody the greater you've seen their behaviour in different circumstances, the more you're able to tell whether what they're saying is correct based on your own experiences. So given that I have only see him relatively briefly, I'm obliged to accept his opinion as being correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you yet formed an opinion of your own in this matter on the particular point? DR. ROWELL: Yes. He claims that it is significant for him, and I have no reason to believe otherwise. I also have no reason to not accept Dr. Eekhof's opinion and Dr. Eekhof has seen him quite extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, how reasonable is it to expect that an individual can resolve what I believe you've characterized as very complicated personal problems? How reasonable is it to expect that a person can resolve such during a short visit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could we add to this question to what extent the medical professional knowledge would enable you to express an expectation that an individual can resolve the problems as you qualify them? So it should be clear from your question, Mr. Groome, and then it would be my question as well, that what the medical profession, whether they could say in advance, "Well, if you go home it will be better or perhaps worse." Is there -- your professional knowledge, could it tell you whether perhaps a direct confrontation with the problems would make it -- would be at risk to make it worse, whereas of course everyone always hopes that matters are going better? I'm asking your assessment not as a normal human being but as from your medical professional point of view. Mr. Groome, would you -- would it still be your question framed -- if phrased this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Could you please answer the question. DR. ROWELL: I don't think from that perspective that anybody can say whether he would get better or get worse, and I don't think that is the medical issue. From the medical perspective all I can say is whether he is sufficiently psychologically capable of dealing with the issues, and whereas a few months ago I would have said that he was not in a position to be able to deal with those issues, now I would say that he was. I cannot tell you. I wouldn't even speculate as to whether this would help or not help, but I would suggest that given he is so enthusiastic about addressing his issues in this way, there is a much higher likelihood of it succeeding. If he was avoiding this issue than there would be a higher likelihood of it failing, so in combination of his psychological state of mind, which is a medical assessment, and his relative enthusiasm, which is just a general assessment, I would say there is a relatively good chance of things going well but ultimately it is still speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any follow-up question in this respective? I would have one but I'd rather put it in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll defer to the Chamber, Your Honour. I was going to ask a slightly different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we turn into private session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One very short question. When you answered the question put to you by Mr. Jordash on observing any deterioration, what situation did you have in mind, where someone is under constant supervision as he is to some extent in the UNDU, or would it also be the same if someone is at home and perhaps comes to hospital twice a week or for an hour or two hours? DR. ROWELL: I think any review will be able to assess his immediate mental state, and people can be seen to improve over the course of days or they can be seen to deteriorate depending on the stressors involved. So if he were to go on provisional release and addressing the issues that he wants to address caused him a great deal of stress, he would start to function less well. He would start to withdraw, and he'd show signs of that, so it could be seen. The same could be true in a detention unit, if there was some stressor that affected his general level of functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if he was not under constant supervision who would then observe the deterioration? Would you see that if he comes for one hour every three days? DR. ROWELL: A clinical review would do it. I don't even think it need to be as much as an hour. Somebody specifically looked at him with -- a medical person with a view to assessing his current mental state, he would tell you whether he was better, worse, or the same than the last time he saw him a few days before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Now, Dr. Rowell, in the report that you filed today, you've assessed that there is -- that Mr. Stanisic is healthy enough physically and psychologically to participate in proceedings up to five hours a day, two days a week; correct? DR. ROWELL: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, on page 84, line 22 of the transcript, you said: "If things went poorly," and I'm referring to provisional release, "right from the start, then the time could be short." I take from that that you recognise that even if Mr. Stanisic's medical regime and current psychiatric regime were maintained perfectly, that there is the possibility that dealing with the personal problems could cause a deterioration in his overall health; correct? DR. ROWELL: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, let's put the personal problems to the side and let me ask you if all the treatments for his physical ailments were abruptly stopped, how soon would you expect to see some objectively observable sign indicating a deterioration in his physical health? DR. ROWELL: I don't think I could really answer that. I'm -- I'm no expert in the details of his medical condition, and I would need to review his medical notes in a great deal more concern that was never an issue for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether it would -- something you would expect rapidly or it would take a number of weeks or months to take place? DR. ROWELL: Again, I think this is a question that's better posed to his gastroenterologist who would be the primary person to comment on the effectiveness of his medications.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you be able to offer a view with respect to whether his -- the same question but if his psychiatric treatment were stopped, would you be able to offer an opinion how soon we would see deterioration? DR. ROWELL: I think it would be seen based on the medications that he's on now over the course of weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Several weeks. DR. ROWELL: One or two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. If there was a deterioration --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. You said you would be brief. It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Rowell missed his appointment already which I really regret. Mr. Groome, last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If there was a deterioration of his physical and psychiatric state while on provisional release to the point where it compromised his able to participate in proceedings, are you able to say how long it would take for his physical and/or psychiatric health to improve to a point where he would once again feel comfortable saying that he's able to participate at the same level you've judged him to be today? DR. ROWELL: I don't think I can -- I can make that assessment. It would all depend on what went wrong, how far backwards he went, and how amenable that problem was to the treatment, which drug and why or which condition and why. So I really can't say, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Rowell. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bench has no further questions for you, Dr. Rowell. We'd like to thank you very much for further -- for the further information you've provided to the Chamber, and we apologise for -- I don't know with whom you had the appointment but the apologies also to that person or persons. Thank you very much for coming. DR. ROWELL: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are about to adjourn. I do understand that the next witness is scheduled for such a short period of time that we could be confident that his testimony could be concluded tomorrow. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gave some instructions to the registrar. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just one brief matter, Your Honour. At the beginning of today's session, the Prosecution tendered map 27 from its map book, a map of Zvornik. Although there was no objection, I don't believe the Chamber has ruled on the matter, so before it gets too far behind us, I'd ask the Chamber to rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, the map is so -- we'll have to -- I hardly see anything on the map that would assist us in the matter apart from that Tuzla is -- is on the map. Apart from that, any other specific reason why -- I mean, it's the only area that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think it also indicates the border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I think it's just to generally orient the Chamber as to the witness's evidence and the other witnesses that testified about Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is -- any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map will be Exhibit number P109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P109 is admitted into evidence. Could we find a way of -- we're now dealing with every single portion of the map admitting it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't understand your last comment. Would you like the Prosecution to identify which portions on the map we specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Whether we should not deal with those maps whatever -- if they're relevant, just admit them unless there's any sort of -- so we have the whole series of maps in evidence. We can look at them whenever it's -- because now we find maps we're supposed not to look at it because not being in evidence yet and then we find perhaps something on it which seems to be relevant for us and then it's not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're meeting tomorrow morning, Your Honour, and we'll discuss that and report to the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps make a selection of -- I'm talking about geographical maps, nothing else. Not about any other matter. If you'd come to an agreement on that it would be appreciated. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is a different subject, Your Honour. It's a return to the provisional release. I'm sorry to leap up at this stage but I was going to do that when Dr. Rowell left to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand -- it's now five minutes past 7.00, and we are already asking far too much from our interpreters and therefore tomorrow, from what I understand, we'll have some time left at the normal --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I imagine that we will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will then further hear from you tomorrow. How much time would you need, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two minutes. Yes, nevertheless not seven minutes past 7.00 to nine minutes past 7.00 but perhaps tomorrow last two minutes before the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And of course the Chamber will consider the matter and will make up its mind before the recess, as far as I can see now, and that would be appropriate, I think. We stand adjourned, and we'll resume tomorrow, the 15th of December, at quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom -- I'm just checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
